items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: We only had four saxophones -- Lester, Jack Washington, Earl.

ctx.x: So now, I'll end this, then we'll go back where we started from. So I kept up with his career after that -- he

never was a successful band leader -- but he made nice records and things and I kept up with him like from -- this must have been about '27. I didn't see him again until I joined Basie's band in 1943. And one night, we were playing at K.U.S. -- State Kansas University and I don't know how many thousand people were listening to the band and there must have been 7 or 800 standing in front of the band and he was standing out there with his arms folded. We only had four saxophones -- Lester, Jack Washington, Earl. So…

items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: And there was Snooky, played the trumpet with Basie at the time, and then Earle Warren

ctx.x: She says, “Mother, I see you’re not going. I’m going with Daddy.” She was about three years old. So she says, “I see you’re not going.” And she says, “but I’m going.” So I couldn’t take her though, at that time of morning, because we were making this picture, I don’t know if it was “Hellzapoppin” with Dorothy Dandridge. Anyway, but she wanted to go. She wanted to go everywhere I’d go. And I remember the night she was born, I wanted to see her to visit, and I was working, it was just about the time we were working…

There’s a story I remember traveling with Basie and at that time they traveled on the trains and this is when they had the berth that you could sleep in. And then you’d have, every morning the wives with the kids of all the musicians would come and we’d come to breakfast. And there was Snooky, played the trumpet with Basie at the time, and then Earle Warren, and I’d have names for all of them. Well musicians have names for each other, Smiley, and Sweets —
